# SHSAT Vocabulary: 2026 Glossary, Roots & Study Tips


**TL;DR:** The SHSAT does not have a standalone vocabulary section. Instead, vocabulary is tested through “in-context” reading comprehension questions that ask what a word means based on the passage, not your memory. This glossary covers the three categories of SHSAT vocabulary you actually need: test-direction terms, high-frequency academic words, and multiple-meaning traps. It also includes a word roots cheat sheet and a proven four-step strategy for answering vocabulary-in-context questions.


---


## How the SHSAT Actually Tests Vocabulary


Here is the single most important thing to understand about SHSAT vocabulary: there is no vocabulary section on the test. You will never see a question that simply asks, “What does this word mean?” Every vocabulary question on the SHSAT is embedded inside a reading comprehension passage, and the correct answer depends on how the word is used in that specific context.


The typical question looks something like this: *“As used in line 12, the word ‘obscure’ most nearly means…”*


That phrasing is a signal. The answer must come from the passage, not from whatever definition you memorized the night before. As Varsity Tutors’ SHSAT lesson explains, many SHSAT words have multiple meanings, so the surrounding sentences always determine which definition applies.


This is why generic vocabulary lists, the kind you find on most Quizlet decks or flashcard apps, are often wasted prep time. Many of those lists include definitions that are technically correct but irrelevant to how the SHSAT uses the word. Practitioners on Reddit’s r/SHSAT community echo this point: the difficulty isn’t in unfamiliar vocabulary but in the precision of questions that force students to distinguish between two seemingly valid answers based on subtle textual evidence.


Not sure where your ELA skills stand? A[diagnostic test](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/diagnostic-test) can help identify your vocabulary and reading comprehension gaps before you start studying.


### The SHSAT ELA Section at a Glance


The SHSAT is a 180-minute, 100-question exam and the sole admissions factor for NYC’s eight specialized high schools. The ELA section contains 50 questions broken into two families:


- **Revising/Editing (standalone and passage-based):** About 7 to 8 questions testing grammar, punctuation, sentence structure, and word choice.
- **Reading Comprehension:** Roughly 42 questions across six passages, covering central idea, inference, text structure, tone, evidence selection, and vocabulary in context.


For the 2026 admissions cycle, 26,123 students took the SHSAT and only 4,023 received offers, an acceptance rate of 15.4%. Starting fall 2025, the test moved to a digital format, and by 2026 it becomes computer-adaptive. The content hasn’t changed, but students can no longer flip back through an entire section freely. That makes strong vocabulary and reading skills even more important because you need to process passages accurately on the first read.


For a full breakdown of score targets by school, see this guide on[SHSAT cutoff scores](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/shsat-cutoff-scores-by-school) .

## Tier 1: Test-Direction Vocabulary


Before worrying about passage words, make sure you understand the language the test itself uses. These are the terms that appear in question stems and answer choices. If you don’t know what “inference” means, you can’t answer an inference question, no matter how strong your reading is.


Term Part of Speech Definition Why It Matters on the SHSAT


**Inference** noun A conclusion drawn from evidence rather than stated directly Many questions ask “What can be inferred from paragraph 3?” You must find something implied, not stated.


**Explicit** adjective Stated directly and clearly Opposite of implicit. If a question asks for explicit information, look for what the passage says outright.


**Implicit** adjective Suggested or implied without being directly stated If something is implicit, you need to read between the lines.


**Connotation** noun The feeling or association a word carries beyond its dictionary definition “Thrifty” and “cheap” mean similar things, but their connotations are very different. Questions about tone often hinge on connotation.


**Denotation** noun The literal dictionary definition of a word The opposite of connotation. Knowing both helps you answer tone and word-choice questions.


**Tone** noun The author’s attitude toward the subject Common answer choices include “critical,” “enthusiastic,” “objective,” “skeptical.”


**Figurative** adjective Using language in a non-literal way (metaphor, simile, personification) If a passage says someone has “a mountain of homework,” the question may ask what the figurative language suggests.


**Literal** adjective The exact, non-figurative meaning Opposite of figurative. Some questions test whether you can tell the difference.


**Rhetoric** noun The art of using language effectively to persuade or inform Questions may ask about “rhetorical purpose” or “rhetorical effect.”


**Theme** noun The central message or underlying meaning of a text Different from topic. The topic might be “war”; the theme might be “the cost of loyalty.”


**Cite** verb To refer to a specific piece of text as evidence “Which sentence best supports the answer to the previous question?” is a cite-evidence question.


**Evidence** noun Details from the text that support a claim or answer You need to point to specific lines, not general impressions.


**Paraphrase** verb To restate something in your own words Correct answer choices often paraphrase the passage rather than quoting it directly.


**Summarize** verb To briefly state the main points Different from paraphrase. A summary covers the whole text; a paraphrase restates a specific part.


**Perspective** noun A particular point of view or way of seeing things Two characters in a passage may have different perspectives on the same event.


**Analogy** noun A comparison between two things to explain or clarify If a passage compares the brain to a computer, that’s an analogy.


**Irony** noun When the actual meaning is opposite to what is said or expected Verbal irony (saying the opposite of what you mean) and situational irony (an unexpected outcome) both appear in SHSAT passages.


**Claim** noun A statement that something is true, usually requiring evidence Informational passages often present a central claim.


**Counterclaim** noun An argument that opposes the main claim Questions may ask you to identify the counterclaim in an argumentative passage.


**Structure** noun How a text is organized Chronological, cause/effect, compare/contrast, problem/solution. Expect questions like “How does the author organize paragraph 4?”


**Chronological** adjective Arranged in the order events happened over time A common text structure, especially in historical or narrative passages.


**Context** noun The surrounding words, sentences, or situation that help clarify meaning This is the foundation of every vocabulary-in-context question.


**Genre** noun A category of literature or writing (fiction, poetry, essay, etc.) Helps you set expectations before you start reading.


**Articulate** verb / adj. (v.) To express clearly; (adj.) able to speak fluently and coherently A test-direction word that also shows up as a passage word.

## Tier 2: High-Frequency SHSAT Academic Words


These are words that appear regularly in the kinds of passages the SHSAT selects: literary fiction, historical nonfiction, science writing, and persuasive essays. They’re drawn from 8th-grade academic vocabulary standards and SHSAT-specific prep materials.


The list is organized into thematic clusters because words are easier to remember when grouped by meaning rather than alphabetically.


### Change and Transformation


Word Part of Speech Definition Example Sentence


**Abolish** verb To formally put an end to The new law sought to abolish the outdated policy.


**Adapt** verb To adjust to new conditions Species that cannot adapt to changing climates face extinction.


**Diminish** verb To make or become less The storm’s power began to diminish as it moved inland.


**Evolve** verb To develop gradually over time The city’s waterfront has evolved from an industrial zone to a public park.


**Obsolete** adjective No longer in use or outdated Typewriters became obsolete after personal computers spread.


**Transform** verb To change completely in form or character The renovation transformed the abandoned warehouse into a community center.


**Fluctuate** verb To rise and fall irregularly Temperatures in the desert fluctuate dramatically between day and night.


### Argument, Persuasion, and Evidence


Word Part of Speech Definition Example Sentence


**Assert** verb To state something confidently and forcefully The researcher asserted that the results were conclusive.


**Concede** verb To admit that something is true after first resisting it Even the harshest critic conceded that the film had stunning visuals.


**Corroborate** verb To confirm or support with evidence The witness’s account corroborated the detective’s theory.


**Refute** verb To prove a statement or theory to be wrong The study refuted the long-held belief that goldfish have three-second memories.


**Substantiate** verb To provide evidence to support a claim She could not substantiate her accusation with any proof.


**Validate** verb To confirm the truth or value of something The experiment was designed to validate the hypothesis.


**Conjecture** noun/verb An opinion formed without complete evidence; to guess His theory was based on conjecture rather than data.


### Emotion, Attitude, and Tone


Word Part of Speech Definition Example Sentence


**Abhor** verb To regard with disgust and hatred She abhors dishonesty in any form.


**Despondent** adjective In low spirits from loss of hope After weeks without news, the family grew despondent.


**Elated** adjective Extremely happy and excited The team was elated after winning the championship.


**Indifferent** adjective Having no particular interest or concern The audience seemed indifferent to the speaker’s arguments.


**Melancholy** noun/adjective A deep, persistent sadness A sense of melancholy pervaded the final chapter.


**Resilient** adjective Able to recover quickly from difficulties The community proved resilient in the aftermath of the flood.


**Somber** adjective Dark, gloomy, or serious in tone The memorial ceremony had a somber atmosphere.


**Apprehensive** adjective Anxious or fearful about something in the future She was apprehensive about starting at a new school.


### Knowledge, Thinking, and Understanding


Word Part of Speech Definition Example Sentence


**Ambiguous** adjective Open to more than one interpretation; unclear The poem’s ending is deliberately ambiguous.


**Astute** adjective Having sharp judgment or keen perception An astute reader will notice the foreshadowing in chapter one.


**Discern** verb To recognize or perceive something It was difficult to discern the speaker’s true intentions.


**Feasible** adjective Possible and practical to accomplish The committee debated whether the plan was financially feasible.


**Ponder** verb To think about something carefully She pondered the question for several minutes before answering.


**Prudent** adjective Acting with care and thought for the future It would be prudent to save some money for emergencies.


**Surmise** verb To suppose something without firm evidence From the muddy footprints, she surmised that someone had been in the garden.


**Scrutinize** verb To examine closely and thoroughly The editor scrutinized every sentence for errors.


### Society, Systems, and Power


Word Part of Speech Definition Example Sentence


**Anarchy** noun A state of disorder due to absence of authority The collapse of the government led to a period of anarchy.


**Boycott** noun/verb To refuse to buy or participate as a protest Activists organized a boycott of the company’s products.


**Confiscate** verb To take or seize with authority The teacher confiscated the student’s phone during the exam.


**Prevalent** adjective Widespread in a particular area or at a particular time Smartphones became prevalent in the early 2010s.


**Imminent** adjective About to happen The dark clouds signaled that a storm was imminent.


**Assimilate** verb To absorb and integrate into a wider group New immigrants often struggle to assimilate into an unfamiliar culture.


**Conscientious** adjective Wishing to do what is right; thorough and careful A conscientious student double-checks their work before submitting.


### Descriptive and General Academic Words


Word Part of Speech Definition Example Sentence


**Abundant** adjective Existing in large quantities; plentiful The region is known for its abundant natural resources.


**Adamant** adjective Refusing to change one’s mind She was adamant that the deadline would not be extended.


**Adept** adjective Very skilled or proficient He became adept at solving complex math problems.


**Adversary** noun An opponent or enemy The two candidates treated each other as adversaries throughout the debate.


**Affluent** adjective Having a great deal of money; wealthy The affluent neighborhood contrasted sharply with the surrounding area.


**Agile** adjective Able to move quickly and easily The gymnast’s agile movements impressed the judges.


**Alleviate** verb To make suffering or a problem less severe The medication helped alleviate her symptoms.


**Audacious** adjective Showing a willingness to take bold risks The audacious escape plan surprised everyone.


**Endeavor** noun/verb An effort to achieve something; to try hard Scientific endeavor has led to remarkable advances in medicine.


Many of these words overlap with SAT vocabulary. Students who build a strong SHSAT vocabulary foundation now will find themselves ahead when they encounter[SAT words in context](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/sat-words-in-context-glossary-tips-practice) in high school.

## Tier 3: Multiple-Meaning Words, the SHSAT’s Favorite Trap


This is where the SHSAT gets tricky. The test loves to pick words you think you know and test a meaning you’ve probably never considered. One SHSAT tutor from Exam Coach puts it well: the goal isn’t to stump you with obscure words but to check whether you can read carefully enough to identify the right meaning in context.


Here are the highest-value multiple-meaning words for SHSAT prep:


Word Common Meaning SHSAT Meaning Example in Context


**Address** A location (123 Main St.) To deal with or speak about The mayor’s speech addressed the city’s housing crisis.


**Assume** To take for granted To take on (a role or responsibility) She assumed leadership of the project after the director resigned.


**Champion** A winner To support or fight for a cause The senator championed funding for public schools.


**Check** To verify To restrain or hold back The heavy snow checked the army’s advance.


**Craft** An art or trade To carefully create (often writing or policy) The lawyer crafted a persuasive argument.


**Critical** Disapproving Extremely important; involving analysis Water access is critical to the region’s survival.


**Deliberate** Done on purpose (adj.) To think about carefully (verb) The jury deliberated for three hours before reaching a verdict.


**Engaged** To be married (or busy) Deeply involved or interested The students were fully engaged in the class discussion.


**Fashion** Clothing trends To make or construct something She fashioned a shelter from fallen branches.


**Flag** A piece of cloth (banner) To weaken, lose energy, or signal for attention His enthusiasm began to flag after the third hour.


**Interest** Curiosity A stake or involvement; also, money earned on a deposit The company had a financial interest in the project’s success.


**Novel** A book (noun) New, original, or unusual (adjective) The scientist proposed a novel approach to the problem.


**Qualify** To meet requirements To limit or make conditional He qualified his praise by noting several areas for improvement.


**Resigned** Quit a job Accepting something undesirable as inevitable She gave a resigned sigh and agreed to stay late.


**Reserved** Booked in advance Slow to reveal emotions; restrained The reserved student rarely spoke up in class but wrote brilliant essays.


**Sound** A noise Reliable, in good condition, or thorough The engineer confirmed the bridge was structurally sound.


**Temper** A person’s mood or anger To soften, moderate, or make less extreme She tempered her criticism with words of encouragement.


**Tender** Soft or gentle To formally offer (verb); also, a form of payment The company tendered a bid for the construction contract.


**Grave** A burial site Serious, giving cause for alarm The doctor’s grave expression worried the family.


**Plot** A secret plan; a story’s events A piece of land The farmer planted corn on a small plot behind the barn.


When you see any of these words on the SHSAT, resist the urge to pick the first meaning that comes to mind. Go back to the passage and check.

## Word Roots, Prefixes, and Suffixes Cheat Sheet


What happens when you encounter a word on the SHSAT that you’ve never seen before? You can’t look it up. But if you recognize parts of the word, you can often figure out its approximate meaning. Most English words are built from Greek and Latin roots, and knowing even a handful of common ones gives you a powerful fallback strategy.


### Essential Prefixes


Prefix Meaning Example Words


**un-** not, opposite unclear, unusual, uncertain


**in- / im- / il- / ir-** not invisible, impossible, illegal, irregular


**dis-** not, opposite, apart disagree, disappear, disrupt


**mis-** wrong, badly mislead, misunderstand, misjudge


**re-** again, back rebuild, reconsider, restore


**pre-** before predict, prevent, precede


**anti-** against antisocial, antibiotic, antiwar


**sub-** under, below submarine, submerge, subordinate


**inter-** between, among international, interact, intervene


**trans-** across, beyond transport, transform, translate


**bene-** good, well benefit, benevolent, benign


**mal-** bad, wrong malfunction, malicious, malnourished


**con- / com-** with, together connect, combine, collaborate


**ex-** out of, former export, exclude, extract


### Essential Roots


Root Meaning Example Words


**dict** speak, say predict, contradict, verdict, dictate


**spec / spect** look, see perspective, inspect, spectacle, specimen


**aud** hear audience, auditory, audible


**cred** believe credible, incredulous, credentials


**chron** time chronological, chronicle, anachronism


**graph / scrib / script** write autobiography, inscribe, manuscript


**port** carry transport, portable, export


**rupt** break interrupt, erupt, disrupt, corrupt


**voc / vok** call, voice vocal, invoke, provoke, advocate


**struct** build construct, structure, instruct, obstruct


**vert / vers** turn convert, reverse, versatile, controversy


**jud / jur / jus** law, judge judge, jury, justice, prejudice


### Common Suffixes


Suffix Meaning Example Words


**-able / -ible** capable of readable, flexible, visible


**-tion / -sion** act or state of education, decision, conclusion


**-ous / -ious** full of, having the quality of courageous, ambitious, mysterious


**-ment** result of, act of achievement, judgment, development


**-less** without hopeless, careless, relentless


**-ful** full of hopeful, powerful, resourceful


**-ist** one who practices or believes scientist, activist, novelist


**-ify / -fy** to make or become simplify, classify, amplify


**How to use this on test day:** If you see the word “incredulous” and don’t know it, break it apart. “In-” means not. “Cred” means believe. “-ulous” is a suffix meaning “tending to.” So “incredulous” means tending not to believe, or skeptical. That’s enough to answer the question.

## How to Study SHSAT Vocabulary Effectively


Memorizing word lists is the least effective way to prepare for SHSAT vocabulary questions. Here’s what actually works, according to both test prep specialists and students who’ve scored well.


### The 4-Step Context Clue Method


Use this strategy every time you encounter a vocabulary-in-context question:


1.


**Read the sentence and its neighbors.** Don’t just read the sentence containing the target word. Read the one before and the one after. Tone, logic, and surrounding details all provide clues.


2.


**Predict a meaning in your own words.** Before looking at the answer choices, come up with your own rough definition. This prevents you from being swayed by tricky options.


3.


**Match your prediction to an answer choice.** Find the choice closest to your prediction.


4.


**Substitute and confirm.** Plug your selected answer back into the original sentence. Does it make sense? Does the paragraph’s meaning stay intact?


The biggest trap on these questions is what tutors call the “most-popular-meaning trap.” The SHSAT often tests a less common definition, and one of the wrong answer choices will be the word’s most familiar meaning, put there specifically to catch students who don’t check the context.


### Four Types of Context Clues to Watch For


- **Synonym clues:** A word with a similar meaning appears nearby. (“The meticulous, detail-oriented architect reviewed every plan.”)
- **Contrast clues:** Signal words like “but,” “however,” “although,” or “unlike” flag the opposite meaning. (“Unlike her gregarious sister, Maya was quiet and withdrawn.”)
- **Definition clues:** The passage directly explains the word. (“Photosynthesis, the process by which plants convert sunlight into energy, occurs in the leaves.”)
- **General context clues:** No single signal word, but reading multiple sentences reveals the meaning. These are the hardest and the most common on the SHSAT.


### Build a Vocabulary Journal


SHSAT tutoring specialists from Ivy Tutors Network recommend a simple practice: look up every unfamiliar word you encounter during practice and write it with its definition in a dedicated section of your notebook. Over weeks, this becomes a personalized vocabulary list far more useful than any generic word bank.


Exam Coach, another SHSAT prep service, suggests introducing a few new words each week through vocabulary journals, word maps, or synonym challenges rather than trying to memorize hundreds of words at once.


### Read Widely and Often


Independent reading is the single best way to build SHSAT vocabulary over time. When students read regularly, they encounter words in natural context, which is exactly how the SHSAT tests them. Good sources for SHSAT-level reading include:


- **The New York Times “Upfront” magazine** (written for students, covers current events)
- **Newsela** (news articles at adjustable reading levels)
- **Short stories and literary fiction** at or above grade level
- **Science magazines** like Scientific American or National Geographic (the SHSAT frequently includes science passages)


Every time you hit an unfamiliar word, pause, guess the meaning from context, then check. This is the 4-step method in real life.


### Use Spaced Repetition


If you do make flashcards, don’t review them all in one sitting. Spaced repetition, reviewing cards at increasing intervals, is the most efficient way to move vocabulary into long-term memory. Free tools that support this include Anki and some features within test prep platforms.


For structured practice that tests vocabulary the way the SHSAT does (in context, not isolation), try working through[practice questions](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/practice-questions) that mirror real test conditions.


### Create a Study Plan


Vocabulary building works best as part of a broader SHSAT preparation strategy, not as an isolated activity. If you’re unsure how to structure your study time across ELA and math, this guide on[how to study for the SHSAT](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/how-to-study-for-the-shsat) breaks the process into manageable steps.

## SHSAT Vocabulary and the Digital Adaptive Format (2026)


Starting with fall 2026 testing, the SHSAT is a computer-adaptive test (CAT). This means the questions you receive are partially determined by how well you’re doing. The vocabulary content itself hasn’t changed, but two things matter for how you study:


**You can’t go back easily.** In the old paper format, you could skip a tricky vocabulary question and return later after reading more of the passage. The digital adaptive format may limit that flexibility. Strong first-read comprehension is more important than ever.


**Precision matters more.** Because the test adapts, getting early questions right unlocks harder (and higher-scoring) questions. Vocabulary-in-context questions that seem straightforward can cost you significant scoring opportunities if you fall for a common-meaning trap.


For updated information on test logistics, check the[SHSAT test dates and registration deadlines](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/shsat-test-dates-registration-deadlines) .

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Does the SHSAT have a vocabulary section?


No. The SHSAT does not include a standalone vocabulary section. Vocabulary is tested only through “vocabulary in context” questions within the reading comprehension portion of the ELA section. These questions ask what a word means as it is used in a specific passage.


### How many vocabulary questions are on the SHSAT?


The exact number varies by test form, but vocabulary-in-context questions are a recurring type within the approximately 42 reading comprehension questions on the ELA section. Expect several per test.


### Should I memorize vocabulary lists for the SHSAT?


Memorizing long word lists is not the best strategy. Because the SHSAT tests vocabulary in context, the most effective preparation is learning to use context clues, building familiarity with academic and multiple-meaning words through regular reading, and practicing with realistic questions. A targeted vocabulary journal beats a 500-word flashcard deck.


### What reading level is the SHSAT?


SHSAT passages are written at approximately 8th to 10th grade reading levels. They include literary fiction, informational nonfiction, historical documents, and science writing. The passages are intentionally varied to test different reading skills.


### Are SHSAT and SAT vocabulary words the same?


There is significant overlap. Both tests favor academic vocabulary and both test words in context rather than in isolation. Students who build strong SHSAT vocabulary habits will find themselves well prepared for the SAT’s Reading and Writing section later. For students already thinking ahead,[digital SAT prep resources](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/digital-sat-prep) cover many of the same vocabulary skills at a higher level.


### What’s the best way to learn vocabulary for the SHSAT?


Combine three approaches: (1) Read widely at or above grade level to encounter words naturally. (2) Keep a vocabulary journal where you write down unfamiliar words with definitions and example sentences. (3) Practice with SHSAT-style passages where vocabulary questions require using context clues. The four-step method (read, predict, match, substitute) is the most reliable test-day strategy.


### How competitive is SHSAT admission?


Very. In 2026, only 15.4% of test-takers received an offer to one of the eight specialized high schools. Cutoffs ranged from 495 at Brooklyn Latin to 561 at Stuyvesant. Every point matters, which is why vocabulary-in-context questions, though they may seem minor, are worth preparing for carefully. See the full breakdown of[score targets by school](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/what-is-a-good-shsat-score-cutoffs-targets) .


### Can practice tests help with SHSAT vocabulary?


Absolutely. Full-length practice tests expose you to the types of passages and vocabulary questions you’ll face on test day. They also help you practice pacing, since spending too long on one vocabulary question can cost time elsewhere. You can access[free SHSAT practice tests](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/best-free-shsat-practice-tests) to start building that experience.
